headline: Nine Hours to Atlantis, a Bigeye at 2 AM, and a Marlin We Didn't Expect
subhead: Full moon current turned the east wall into a conveyor belt this week — yellowfin by day, bigeye by chunk, and the first real white marlin bite of the summer.
body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 4 AM Tuesday with the tank full and the fuel log started, because that's how you run to Atlantis — you don't leave anything to chance on a hundred-mile-plus round trip. Call it a hundred nautical miles each way from Montauk, nine hours of running time if the sea stays honest, and somewhere north of three hundred gallons burned by the time you tie back up. That math doesn't change whether the fishing is good or bad, so you plan for it before you ever look at a temp break.

What we found on the east wall was worth the diesel. The moon's full right now, which means the current on that ledge was running harder than it has in weeks, and a hard-running current on a canyon wall does what it always does — it pins bait against structure and makes everything downstream of it nervous. We trolled the 100-fathom curve down through the canyon head starting around first light, small tuna feathers and a naked bird spread at 6 to 7 knots, and had yellowfin all morning. Nothing giant — fifty to seventy pounds, the class fish we've been seeing all month — but they were there consistently enough that we never had to search hard. The color change was sharp, green water pinched right up against the blue, and every time we crossed it we got bit.

Around 10 AM we had a mahi come up under a mat of sargassum sitting off the edge, small school, nothing over ten pounds, but a nice distraction while we reset the spread. Then just after noon, on the long rigger, we hooked into something that took drag in that slow, deliberate way that isn't a yellowfin — a white marlin, and a good one, greyhounding twice before we got a leader touch and let her go. That's the first real marlin action I've had out there this season, and it lines up with what we'd been hearing — the numbers were supposed to start building by mid-August, and this week they did.

We fished the troll hard through the afternoon and then set up to chunk the night tide, and this is where the moon actually worked in our favor instead of against us. We'd talked last week about how a soft current trims the chunk bite down to almost nothing, and how the smarter play in that situation is to troll the break all day and save your chunking for the strongest tide of the night rather than commit to a full all-night drift hoping it turns on. This week the current was the opposite problem — too strong for most of the evening — but the same logic held. We waited for the tide to slack toward the second half of the night, around 1 AM, dropped butterfish chunks on 50-wide outfits with 6/0 circle hooks and no leader wire, just 60-pound fluoro, and connected on a bigeye a little after 2 AM. Not a giant — call it 180 pounds — but a bigeye off Atlantis on a August night bite is a fish you don't complain about, especially after running nine hours to get there.

Bluefin sign was scattered rather than concentrated — we marked fish on structure a few times on the sounder but never got a jumper or a real feeding frenzy to key on. That's consistent with what boats working Veatch and Hydrographer this week have described too — bluefin are around, they're just not schooled up tight enough yet to build a program around. If you're going to target them specifically right now, I'd fish structure edges early and late and not expect a blitz.

Water out at the canyons is holding warm — high 70s on the surface out toward the shelf break, warmer than the water right off Montauk Point, which is still in the mid-70s. That gradient is exactly what's pinning the warm-water species — yellowfin, mahi, marlin — up against the edge instead of letting them spread out over open water. As long as that edge holds its position, the bite should stay consistent enough to plan a trip around, though I wouldn't call it easy. We worked for every one of those yellowfin, and the marlin bite is still building, not blown wide open.

Looking ahead, the moon comes off full over the next few days and that should ease the current back toward something more normal, which usually settles bite windows into tighter, more predictable stretches rather than the all-day grind we had this week. If I had one more trip to plan before the pattern shifts, I'd run to Atlantis or Veatch, troll the wall hard from first light through early afternoon while the yellowfin are up and moving, and hold the chunk gear for the back half of the night tide rather than committing to it early. Keep an eye on the wider tropics too — nothing imminent that I've seen, but late August is when a stray system can push swell into these grounds fast, and a hundred miles offshore is not where you want to be guessing about that.
